alt: Three tools: a theory explains how politics works, a model simplifies one part into categories such as hard, soft and smart power, and an analytical framework structures questions, such as looking at different scales. They organise, simplify, explain, predict, prescribe and evaluate.
caption: Theories explain, models sort, frameworks structure the questions.

alt: A comparison table. Realism starts from anarchy and self-help, focuses on states and relative gains, and uses ideas such as the security dilemma; thinkers include Morgenthau, Waltz and Mearsheimer. Liberalism accepts anarchy but sees cooperation through institutions, many actors and absolute gains, with complex interdependence and democratic peace; Keohane and Nye are key.
caption: Relative versus absolute gains is the hinge between realism and liberalism.

alt: Social constructivism holds that ideas, identities and norms shape interests, as in Wendt’s 1992 article and the landmine campaign. Feminism makes gender a category of analysis, citing Enloe and UN Resolution 1325. Postcolonialism studies how colonialism still shapes the world, citing Said’s Orientalism and Mignolo.
caption: Critical theories ask what ideas, gender and colonial history do to global politics.

alt: Left, realism’s security dilemma: A arms for defence, B sees a threat and arms, A sees a threat in turn, and everyone ends up less safe. Right, constructivism: norm entrepreneurs such as the International Campaign to Ban Landmines spread a new norm that led to the 1997 Ottawa Treaty.
caption: Realism explains spirals of fear; constructivism explains how new norms take hold.

after: ## How each perspective reads the key concepts
alt: A grid of how realism, liberalism, constructivism, feminism and postcolonialism read power, sovereignty, legitimacy and interdependence; for example realism sees power as material and relative, while postcolonialism sees it as built on historical hierarchy. R2P is read as norm change by constructivists and as selective power by realists.
caption: Each lens reads the same key concept differently.

after: ## Worked example: one case, five lenses
alt: The 2015 Paris Agreement read through five perspectives: realism (self-set targets protect sovereignty), liberalism (reporting and review build cooperation), constructivism (climate action as a norm of responsible statehood), feminism (who decides and who bears the cost) and postcolonialism (historical emissions and differentiated responsibilities).
caption: Saying which lens explains which part of a case is the evaluation.

alt: Four parts of a theory paragraph, using the COVID-19 pandemic: a realist claim that states protect their own first; the case of export restrictions on vaccines and supplies; a link to sovereignty and national interest; and a limit, with COVAX as a liberal counterpoint and a postcolonial point that lower-income states waited longest.
caption: Claim, case, key concept, limit: then turn to another lens.
